soundness.reasons: B more directly separates reproducibility from correctness by using exact attributions for the same fixed-background game, while A evaluates agreement only with reruns. evidence.quote: \textbf{Verdict.} The answer to ``can a single run be taken as the basis of the prediction?'' is conditional. For the \emph{top-1} claim, yes at almost any budget $\ge$256 on our data (98\%+ correct). For the \emph{top-3 set}, yes at $m\approx2048$ for most instances (98.4\% of runs; 94\% of instances meet a 90\% repeatability bar) but not at $m\le256$ for a fifth of instances, and not for the near-tie instances (about one in five at $d\ge16$) at any budget---there the question is ill-posed rather than under-sampled. For complete enumeration ($d\lesssim10$) there is no noise to worry about. A single run is also adequate in a more relative sense: coalition noise is much smaller than the changes due to retraining or the background draw. What fails is not the single run itself but unverified single runs: a free within-run $z$ statistic identifies the runs that cannot be trusted, and the \texttt{shap} defaults may bias the result in a way no repetition would reveal.

A run errs on the top-3 set when noise reorders the 3rd and 4th largest attributions. If the estimate were Gaussian with the empirical SD $\sigma_j$ of each feature, the probability of preserving the order is $\approx\Phi(z)$ with $z=(a_{(3)}-a_{(4)})/\sqrt{\sigma_{(3)}^2+\sigma_{(4)}^2}$. Fig.~\ref{fig:mech}a shows this holds empirically: instance-by-budget cells from all five datasets, four models and all budgets lie close to $\Phi(z)$, regardless of $d$ (the observed probability is slightly below $\Phi(z)$ for $z\lesssim2$, e.g.\ 0.54 vs.\ 0.60 at $z\approx0.25$: the Gaussian two-feature approximation is mildly optimistic). The practical consequence is that the budget needed is set by the \emph{instance's} margin: the gap between the 3rd and 4th attribution relative to the run-to-run noise, where the noise shrinks faster than $m^{-1/2}$ (by a factor of about 1.5 per doubling of $m$ from $m{=}256$, since larger budgets also enumerate more size classes; Appendix Fig.~\ref{fig:sd}). At $m{=}2048$, 19.6\% of the $d\ge16$ instance--model pairs have a gap below $0.02\|\phi\|_2$, and \emph{all 18} pairs that fail the 90\% criterion are among them (Fig.~\ref{fig:mech}b): failures are near-ties. In those cases the claim ``these are the top three features'' is not well determined by the model's exact attribution either, so resolving them with more compute has little value. The noise level itself is tied to non-additivity: the share of the kernel-weighted variance of $v$ left unexplained by the additive game correlates with the relative run-to-run SD (Spearman 0.64 at $m{=}512$, $d\ge16$, 336 instance--model pairs; 0.70 within ACSEmployment, 0.51 within German).

Fig.~\ref{fig:budget} and Table~\ref{tab:rel} (Appendix) give the main picture. For the two datasets with $d\ge16$, pooled over the 8 (dataset, model) cells, a Kernel SHAP run at $m{=}2048$ (the default budget is $m{=}2d{+}2048$) names the exact top-1 feature in 99.4\% [99.0, 99.8] of runs and the exact top-3 set in 98.4\% [97.7, 99.1], with mean relative $\ell_2$ error 1.4\%. Run-to-run agreement of the top-3 set between two independent runs is 97.6\% [96.5, 98.5] at $m{=}2048$ and 90.1\% [88.0, 92.1] at $m{=}256$ (Nogueira stability 0.991 and 0.960; this measure is lenient here because only two or three features fluctuate between ranks).

Our answer depends on the configuration. A single run of KernelSHAP with $\ell_1$ selection off and paired sampling at a small budget returns the exact top-3 set in at least nine of ten runs for 92--95\% of instances on every cell of both tasks (Table~\ref{tab:reliable}), so for the models we tested one run of a corrected estimator is a reasonable basis for a top-3 explanation. soundness.reasons: Both answer a meaningful, explicitly restricted version of the task: fidelity of a budgeted explanation to a fixed empirical game, rather than validity of the underlying decision. Their code separates training from audit cases, fits preprocessing on training data, preserves original-feature groups, and evaluates fixed budget grids against appropriate controls. A offers stronger deployment grounding through actual library calls, uncached latency measurements and repeated independent background redraws; B offers an independent-path control, chance-corrected subset stability and paired simultaneous contrast bands. Both preserve case dependence in inference and state that their small empirical backgrounds and conditional analyses do not support population or decision-safety guarantees. These complementary strengths do not establish a clear methodological winner.
